cards.front: Cell-cycle non-specific vs cell-cycle specific cytotoxic drugs: give one example of each and the key difference.
cards.back: Non-specific drugs kill resting as well as dividing cells (e.g. alkylating agents, cisplatin, anthracyclines, actinomycin D). Specific drugs kill only cycling cells, usually in one phase (e.g. antimetabolites in S phase, vinca alkaloids and taxanes in M phase).

cards.front: Why are cell-cycle specific drugs given in short pulses, and where do they sit in a regimen?
cards.back: Resting cells are less drug-sensitive and re-enter the cycle between courses, so repeated pulses catch more of the tumour. Specific drugs are usually scheduled after a course of non-specific drugs to improve the kill.

cards.front: Why do large solid tumours respond poorly to cytotoxic drugs compared with leukaemias and lymphomas?
cards.back: Most large solid tumours have a low growth fraction, so few cells are dividing at any moment and cycle-dependent drugs have fewer targets. Leukaemias and lymphomas have a high growth fraction and respond better.

cards.front: Complete: phase of action of selected anticancer drugs.
cards.text: Methotrexate and fluorouracil act mainly in the {{S phase}}; vinca alkaloids and taxanes act in the {{M phase}}; bleomycin and the topoisomerase inhibitors act in {{G2}}; etoposide is listed by KDT under both {{G1 and G2}}.

cards.front: How do tumours become resistant to a drug used repeatedly, and what is the main multidrug resistance mechanism?
cards.back: Repeated use of a single drug, especially at low dose, selects for less sensitive clones. Mutations in the target give drug-specific resistance. Overexpression of the MDR1 gene raises P-glycoprotein, an efflux pump that expels vinca alkaloids, anthracyclines and taxanes.

cards.front: Which malignancies can chemotherapy cure or put into long remission, and which does it only palliate?
cards.back: Cure or long remission: childhood acute leukaemias, Wilms tumour, Ewing sarcoma, retinoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, choriocarcinoma, Hodgkin and Burkitt lymphoma, testicular teratoma and seminoma, mycosis fungoides. Palliation (shrinks tumour, prolongs life): breast, ovary, endometrium, prostate, myeloma, CLL, CML, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, small cell lung and head and neck cancers.

cards.front: Essay: Principles of combination cancer chemotherapy

points: A single drug seldom cures; combinations give greater total kill
Each drug kills a fixed fraction of cells, so more drugs leave fewer survivors
Intensive regimens early in disease work best
Each agent active when used alone
Different mechanisms and different toxicities
Non-overlapping resistance mechanisms
Known synergy, e.g. 5-FU with leucovorin, or with cisplatin or oxaliplatin
Kinetic scheduling: non-specific drugs first, then cycle-specific drugs in pulses
Pulses 2 to 3 weeks apart let normal tissue recover, while tumour cells recover more slowly
About 6 to 11 cycles may be needed; maintenance after that adds no further benefit
Palliative: large tumour burden shrinks
Adjuvant: clears micrometastases after surgery or radiotherapy
Combined modality with surgery, radiation and immunotherapy
ABVD for Hodgkin disease
CHOP-R for non-Hodgkin lymphoma
BEP for testicular cancer
FOLFOX and FOLFIRI for colorectal cancer

cards.front: Essay: General toxicities of cytotoxic drugs and their supportive care

points: Granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia and anaemia; usually the dose-limiting toxicity
Consequences: infection and bleeding
Lymphocytopenia and loss of cell-mediated and humoral immunity
Opportunistic infection: Candida and other deep mycoses, herpes zoster, CMV, Pneumocystis, Toxoplasma
Mucositis with fluorouracil, methotrexate, anthracyclines, bleomycin, actinomycin D; xerostomia and caries
Nausea and vomiting from direct chemoreceptor and upper GI effects
Diarrhoea and mucosal shedding
Alopecia and dermatitis
Oligospermia, impotence, amenorrhoea
Teratogenic and abortifacient in pregnancy
Secondary leukaemias and lymphomas years later
Hyperuricaemia from massive cell death, especially in leukaemias and bulky lymphomas: acute renal failure, gout, urate stones
Allopurinol, urinary alkalinisation and generous fluids protect; corticosteroids also lower uric acid
Rasburicase (urate oxidase) i.v. for acute hyperuricaemia in haematological malignancy at risk of rapid lysis
Antiemetics; G-CSF or GM-CSF to shorten neutropenia
Platelet and granulocyte transfusion when needed
Mesna, leucovorin, dexrazoxane and amifostine as specific protectors

cards.front: Why is cisplatin highly emetogenic, and what is the antiemetic approach?
cards.back: Cisplatin stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone directly and also generates emetic signals from the upper GI tract, so antiemetics are given routinely before each infusion. Ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) has surpassed metoclopramide; adding dexamethasone and/or lorazepam or aprepitant (NK1 antagonist) gives further protection.

cards.front: How do alkylating agents damage DNA, and what is their cell-cycle profile?
cards.back: They form reactive carbonium ions that covalently alkylate macromolecules, most often at guanine N7. The result is cross-linking, abnormal base pairing or strand breaks. They are radiomimetic and mostly cell-cycle non-specific.

cards.front: Cyclophosphamide: why is it not directly toxic, and what are its characteristic toxicities?
cards.back: It is a prodrug, activated by hepatic CYP enzymes to aldophosphamide, which splits into phosphoramide mustard (the antitumour alkylator) and acrolein. Acrolein causes haemorrhagic cystitis, so vigorous hydration is needed at high doses and mesna protects the bladder. Alopecia is prominent. It spares platelets better than many alkylators and is strongly immunosuppressive.

cards.front: Ifosfamide versus cyclophosphamide, and why is mesna given with ifosfamide?
cards.back: Ifosfamide has a longer, dose-dependent half-life and causes more neurotoxicity (confusion, hallucinations, seizures, coma) and haemorrhagic cystitis, but less alopecia and less emesis. Mesna is a sulfhydryl compound excreted in urine that binds the bladder-toxic metabolites and protects the bladder.

cards.front: Complete: uses of selected alkylating agents.
cards.text: Chlorambucil was historically used almost only for {{chronic lymphatic leukaemia}}, but first-line CLL therapy now relies on drugs that modulate B-cell receptor signalling; busulfan, the most myeloid-selective alkylator, was standard for chronic-phase {{CML}} before imatinib and is now valued mainly in high-dose therapy before {{stem cell transplant}}; {{temozolomide}}, with radiotherapy, is the standard initial drug for {{high-grade gliomas}}.

cards.front: Short note: Cisplatin

points: Hydrolysed inside cells to a reactive species that cross-links DNA, mainly at guanine N7
Also binds sulfhydryl groups of proteins
Enters via the copper transporter CTR1; resistance from efflux (MRP1) and altered transport
Metastatic testicular and ovarian cancer
Lung, bladder, oesophagus, stomach, liver, head and neck cancers
Cumulative, dose-dependent nephrotoxicity (the main problem)
Electrolyte wasting from tubular damage: hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia; can cause tetany
Highly emetic; tinnitus, deafness, sensory neuropathy, hyperuricaemia
Shock-like reaction during infusion
Saline hydration before and after infusion (about 1 to 2 L); routine plasma Mg2+ measurement
Antiemetic cover
Amifostine, a thiophosphate activated by alkaline phosphatase, for nephro- and neurotoxicity

cards.front: Carboplatin and oxaliplatin: how do their toxicity profiles differ from cisplatin?
cards.back: Carboplatin has less nephro-, oto- and neurotoxicity and milder, delayed emesis; its dose-limiting toxicity is thrombocytopenia. Oxaliplatin's dose-limiting toxicity is peripheral neuropathy, with an acute form triggered by cold. It is not affected by cisplatin resistance and synergises with fluorouracil in colorectal cancer.

cards.front: Short note: Methotrexate

points: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so tetrahydrofolate is not regenerated
Retained in cells as polyglutamates; also inhibits thymidylate synthase
S-phase specific
Choriocarcinoma (can be curative)
Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (high dose with rescue)
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, breast, bladder, head and neck, osteosarcoma
Immunosuppression in rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis
Megaloblastic anaemia with low repeated doses; pancytopenia with high doses
Mucositis, diarrhoea, GI bleeding
High dose: renal toxicity from drug precipitation in acid urine, so hydrate and alkalinise urine beforehand
Long-term low dose: cirrhosis; also pneumonitis, teratogenicity
Salicylates, sulfonamides and dicoumarol displace it from plasma proteins
Aspirin and sulfonamides cut its renal tubular secretion and raise toxicity
Folinic acid (leucovorin) reverses toxicity; folic acid does not
Glucarpidase, a methotrexate-cleaving enzyme, is approved to treat toxicity

cards.front: Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue: why does it work after high-dose methotrexate when folic acid does not, and how is it given?
cards.back: Methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase, so folic acid cannot be converted to the active coenzyme. Folinic acid (N5-formyl tetrahydrofolate) is a fully reduced folate, so it bypasses the block and refills the tetrahydrofolate pool. High-dose methotrexate is given only if leucovorin rescue follows within 24 hours of the infusion; if the methotrexate level is still high at 48 hours, larger leucovorin doses are continued until it falls. Normal cells are said to be rescued more than tumour cells, which widens the therapeutic index. Leucovorin does not reverse methotrexate neurotoxicity.

cards.front: Short note: Thiopurines (mercaptopurine and thioguanine)

points: Converted to nucleotides that block purine synthesis
Incorporated into DNA and RNA, causing dysfunction
Partial feedback inhibition of de novo purine synthesis
Childhood acute leukaemia: induction with thioguanine and maintenance with mercaptopurine
Choriocarcinoma and some solid tumours
Xanthine oxidase degrades mercaptopurine and azathioprine: with allopurinol the dose must be cut to about one-quarter to one-third (GG14: reduce oral mercaptopurine by 75%)
Thioguanine is not a xanthine oxidase substrate: no dose change
TPMT methylates both; TPMT deficiency or polymorphism causes severe, prolonged myelosuppression; TPMT overexpression causes resistance
Slowly developing bone marrow depression
Mercaptopurine: more nausea and vomiting, reversible jaundice
Hyperuricaemia with both

cards.front: Fluorouracil: how does it block DNA synthesis, what modulates it, and what determines its toxicity?
cards.back: Its nucleotide FdUMP forms a covalent ternary complex with thymidylate synthase and methylene-tetrahydrofolate, irreversibly blocking thymidylate synthesis. Its triphosphate is also incorporated into RNA. Leucovorin enhances the effect, and cisplatin or oxaliplatin synergise (FOLFOX). It is inactivated by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD); DPD deficiency causes severe toxicity, which can be rescued with uridine triacetate. Capecitabine is an oral prodrug converted to fluorouracil by thymidine phosphorylase, an enzyme rich in many breast and colorectal tumours.

cards.front: Cytarabine: which cancers respond, why is it given as repeated boluses or infusion, and what is its main toxicity?
cards.back: Used for induction in acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukaemia, blast crisis of CML and non-Hodgkin lymphoma; ineffective in solid tumours. It is S-phase specific and is rapidly deaminated, so it is given as repeated i.v. bolus or continuous infusion over days. Toxicity: marrow suppression, mucositis, diarrhoea and delayed pulmonary complications.

cards.front: L-asparaginase: mechanism, and why its toxicity profile differs from other cytotoxic drugs.
cards.back: It hydrolyses circulating L-asparagine, starving asparagine-dependent leukaemic cells. It lacks marrow, alopecia and mucosal toxicity, but causes effects of defective protein synthesis: hyperglycaemia, raised triglycerides, pancreatitis, liver damage, clotting defects and CNS effects. Hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis occur, and neutralising antibodies limit repeat use; the PEG-conjugated form lasts longer and is less antigenic.

cards.front: Short note: Vinca alkaloids (vincristine and vinblastine)

points: Bind tubulin and block microtubule assembly
Disrupts the mitotic spindle: metaphase arrest
M-phase specific
Rapid remission in childhood ALL; poor for maintenance
Also acute myeloid leukaemia, Hodgkin, Wilms, Ewing, neuroblastoma, lung
Peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, autonomic effects (postural hypotension, paralytic ileus, urinary retention); little marrow depression
Hodgkin disease, Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular and breast cancer
More marrow depression, less neurotoxicity and alopecia
Local necrosis if extravasated
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion can occur with both

cards.front: How do taxanes differ mechanistically from vinca alkaloids?
cards.back: Taxanes bind beta-tubulin and promote excess polymerisation while stabilising microtubules against depolymerisation. Vinca alkaloids do the opposite. Both arrest mitosis, but taxanes produce abnormal microtubule bundles throughout the cell cycle.

cards.front: Short note: Paclitaxel

points: Diterpene taxane from yew bark
Given in a polyoxyethylated castor oil vehicle, which causes anaphylactoid reactions
Dexamethasone plus H1 and H2 antihistamines before each dose
Ovarian cancer (with cisplatin or carboplatin) and breast cancer; KDT lists use after first-line failure
Head and neck, small cell lung, oesophageal, bladder and prostate cancer
AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma
Reversible granulocytopenia
Stocking-and-glove neuropathy; arthralgia, myalgia, mucositis, oedema
Docetaxel is more potent, uses a polysorbate vehicle (fewer hypersensitivity reactions), causes more neutropenia and less neuropathy

cards.front: Etoposide versus topotecan and irinotecan: which enzyme does each act on?
cards.back: Etoposide inhibits topoisomerase II (G2 arrest) and prevents resealing of DNA breaks. Topotecan and irinotecan inhibit topoisomerase I, leaving single-strand breaks that become lethal during replication. Irinotecan is a prodrug activated to SN-38; its inactivation depends on UGT1A1, and the UGT1A1*28 allele raises the risk of diarrhoea and neutropenia. Irinotecan can cause early cholinergic effects, which atropine suppresses.

cards.front: Short note: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity and its prevention

points: Intercalate DNA and poison topoisomerase II
Generate quinone-type free radicals
ECG changes and arrhythmias within days; brief and usually reversible
Rarely an acute pericarditis-myocarditis syndrome with heart failure
Cumulative, dose-related cardiomyopathy and congestive heart failure; mortality of established CHF approaches 50%
Usual total-dose limit for doxorubicin about 550 mg/m2 (risk up to about 20% at that dose); about 300 mg/m2 in children; KDT notes toxicity usually above 300 mg/m2
Epirubicin: risk rises sharply above 900 mg/m2
Risk is higher with cardiac irradiation, high-dose cyclophosphamide or trastuzumab; heart failure can appear years later
Keep within total-dose limits
Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator infused before doxorubicin, reduces cardiotoxicity but may lower anticancer efficacy; also used for extravasation
Idarubicin and mitoxantrone are less cardiotoxic (mitoxantrone forms few quinone free radicals)

cards.front: Complete: cytotoxic antibiotics and their key features.
cards.text: Mitomycin C is now used mainly in {{anal cancer}} and intravesically for {{superficial bladder tumours}}; bleomycin causes {{pulmonary fibrosis}} with little {{myelosuppression}}; actinomycin D is used in {{Wilms' tumour}} and childhood {{rhabdomyosarcoma}}.

cards.front: Imatinib: which kinases does it block, and which tumours respond?
cards.back: It inhibits the Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase of CML and also PDGF receptor and c-KIT. It is the drug of choice for metastatic c-KIT-positive GIST, and produces remission in over 90% of chronic-phase CML. It is also used in dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. Resistance arises from point mutations in Bcr-Abl.

cards.front: Complete: newer kinase inhibitors.
cards.text: Dasatinib and nilotinib are second-generation {{Bcr-Abl}} inhibitors for CML resistant to or intolerant of imatinib, and nilotinib is now also used first-line; both can cause {{QT prolongation}}, and dasatinib can cause pleural effusion. Sunitinib and sorafenib are oral multi-kinase inhibitors that block the {{VEGF receptor}}, used in {{renal cell carcinoma}}; sorafenib is also approved for hepatocellular and thyroid cancer, and sunitinib for imatinib-resistant GIST.

cards.front: Gefitinib: which lung cancer patients respond, and what are its key adverse effects?
cards.back: It is an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor effective mainly in non-small cell lung cancer with activating EGFR mutations (exon 19 deletions or the exon 21 L858R mutation), which are commoner in non-smokers and women. Common effects are skin rash and diarrhoea; interstitial lung disease is uncommon but serious. It is metabolised by CYP3A4. The third-generation inhibitor osimertinib is approved first-line for these mutations and for tumours that acquire the T790M resistance mutation.

cards.front: Trastuzumab: target, main indications, and what must be monitored?
cards.back: A humanised monoclonal antibody against the extracellular domain of HER2. Used in HER2-positive breast cancer and HER2-positive gastric cancer, usually with a taxane. Acute infusion reactions (fever, chills, dyspnoea) are common. Cardiotoxicity: LVEF falls in under 5% and symptomatic heart failure occurs in under 1%, but the risk rises to about 20% when combined with doxorubicin, so LVEF is monitored during and after treatment.

cards.front: Rituximab: target antigen, how it kills cells, and key adverse effects.
cards.back: A chimeric anti-CD20 antibody acting on B cells. It kills by inducing apoptosis, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement-dependent cytotoxicity. Used in B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, CLL and autoimmune diseases. Adverse effects: infusion reactions (reduce by slow escalation of rate and antihistamines), B-cell depletion, late neutropenia, tumour lysis when the tumour burden is high, reactivation of hepatitis B and JC polyomavirus, and rare severe mucocutaneous reactions.

cards.front: Essay: Targeted anticancer therapy

points: Attacks specific pathways or surface antigens rather than all dividing cells
Small molecules are oral; monoclonal antibodies are given parenterally
Some tumours still respond poorly, and resistance can develop
Imatinib: Bcr-Abl, PDGF receptor, c-KIT
Dasatinib and nilotinib: second-generation Bcr-Abl inhibitors
Gefitinib, erlotinib: EGFR, in mutant lung cancer
Sunitinib, sorafenib: VEGF receptor and other kinases
Trastuzumab: HER2 (breast, gastric); cardiac monitoring needed
Cetuximab: EGFR (head and neck, colorectal); acneiform rash, hypomagnesaemia
Bevacizumab: VEGF-A; hypertension, arterial thromboembolism, bleeding, GI perforation, poor wound healing
Rituximab: CD20 on B cells
Bortezomib: boron-containing; stops NF-kB release, so survival signals fall
Used in multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma
Peripheral neuropathy most prominent; thrombocytopenia also
Resistance through target mutation
Multi-kinase inhibitors have wider adverse effects
Anti-angiogenics carry bleeding and healing risks

cards.front: Why are glucocorticoids used in cancer therapy, and what limits their use?
cards.back: Their lympholytic action makes them key in acute childhood leukaemia and lymphomas: remission is rapid but relapse eventually occurs. They also help in Hodgkin disease, manage complications such as hypercalcaemia, haemolysis, retinoic acid syndrome, raised intracranial pressure and mediastinal oedema, and potentiate antiemetics. Long-term corticosteroid toxicity limits use.

cards.front: Complete: hormonal drug classes for breast cancer.
cards.text: The three main classes are {{selective oestrogen receptor modulators}} such as tamoxifen, {{selective oestrogen receptor down-regulators}} such as fulvestrant, and {{aromatase inhibitors}} such as letrozole; they form the backbone of adjuvant and palliative breast cancer hormone therapy.

cards.front: Where do estrogens, antiandrogens, GnRH analogues and progestins fit in cancer therapy?
cards.back: Estrogens give symptomatic relief in prostate cancer but have been superseded by GnRH agonists used with an antiandrogen. Antiandrogens (flutamide, bicalutamide) raise androgen secretion by blocking pituitary feedback, so they need orchiectomy or a GnRH analogue for full effect. Progestins give temporary remission in endometrial cancer at high doses and are used palliatively in breast cancer no longer responding to tamoxifen. Finasteride and dutasteride are occasionally used in advanced prostate cancer.

cards.front: Cyclosporine: how does it suppress T-cell activation?
cards.back: It binds cyclophilin, and the complex inhibits calcineurin. NFAT then cannot enter the nucleus, so IL-2 and other cytokine genes are not transcribed and the helper T-cell response fails. It spares marrow and humoral immunity, mainly suppressing cell-mediated immunity. It is most active when given before antigen exposure.

cards.front: Short note: Cyclosporine toxicity and drug interactions

points: Main dose-limiting problem
Also impairs liver function
Sustained hypertension and diabetes
Hyperkalaemia, hyperuricaemia, hirsutism, gum hyperplasia
Tremor, seizures, anorexia, lethargy, opportunistic infection
Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B and NSAIDs
Reduced renal function slows excretion of other drugs
Enzyme inducers (phenytoin, phenobarbitone, rifampin) lower levels: risk of rejection
CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole) raise levels: toxicity
Potassium supplements and potassium-sparing diuretics cause marked hyperkalaemia

cards.front: Why does cyclosporine need blood-level monitoring, and why is a microemulsion formulation preferred?
cards.back: Oral absorption is variable and depends on bile, so the older soft-gelatin capsules were erratic. The microemulsion gives more consistent bioavailability. It is metabolised by CYP3A4 and excreted in bile, with a biphasic half-life. The intravenous form uses a polyoxyethylated castor oil vehicle that causes chills, fever and dyspnoea, so it is reserved for emergencies.

cards.front: Tacrolimus versus cyclosporine: what is shared, what differs, and why is tacrolimus often preferred?
cards.back: Both inhibit calcineurin through an immunophilin: cyclophilin for cyclosporine, FKBP for tacrolimus. Tacrolimus is a macrolide about 100 times more potent. It is preferred in transplantation for potency and easier monitoring, and its absorption does not depend on bile, which suits liver transplant. It causes more diabetes, neurotoxicity, alopecia and diarrhoea, and less hypertension, hirsutism and gum hyperplasia. Its dose-limiting toxicity is renal.

cards.front: Short note: Sirolimus and everolimus (mTOR inhibitors)

points: Binds FKBP like tacrolimus, but the complex inhibits mTOR, not calcineurin
Acts later in the IL-2 signalling cascade, so it is antiproliferative
CYP3A4 handles it; cyclosporine raises its levels
Kidney transplant prophylaxis and rescue, often in calcineurin-sparing combinations with mycophenolate and steroid
Not recommended for liver transplant
Coated stents to limit restenosis
Not nephrotoxic
Thrombocytopenia, raised lipids, diarrhoea, liver damage, pneumonitis, impaired wound healing
Better and more consistent oral absorption; shorter half-life
Transplant use in kidney and liver
Also used in advanced renal cell cancer, HR-positive HER2-negative breast cancer and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours

cards.front: Complete: temsirolimus.
cards.text: Temsirolimus is an intravenous {{ester}} of sirolimus that is converted in the body to {{sirolimus}}, an mTOR inhibitor; it is used in advanced {{renal cell carcinoma}} and refractory {{mantle cell lymphoma}}.

cards.front: Azathioprine: how is it activated, and what are its main immunosuppressive uses?
cards.back: It is a prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine and taken up preferentially by immune cells. It blocks purine synthesis and DNA function, mainly suppressing cell-mediated immunity. Uses: transplant rejection (less effective than cyclosporine, so usually combined with it or used when cyclosporine is toxic), low doses in rheumatoid arthritis, maintenance in inflammatory bowel disease, and vitiligo. Key interaction: allopurinol blocks its breakdown by xanthine oxidase, so the dose must be cut to about one-quarter to one-third.

cards.front: What is the role of TPMT in azathioprine and thiopurine therapy, and what happens in TPMT deficiency?
cards.back: Thiopurine methyltransferase methylates the thiopurines as an alternative metabolic route. Genetic deficiency raises the risk of myelosuppression, mucositis and gut damage with mercaptopurine and increases azathioprine toxicity; with a TPMT polymorphism, myelosuppression can be severe and prolonged. Overexpression of TPMT is a cause of thiopurine resistance in leukaemic cells.

cards.front: Mycophenolate mofetil: which enzyme does it inhibit, and why do lymphocytes depend on it?
cards.back: It is a prodrug of mycophenolic acid, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, the key enzyme of de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis. T and B cells lack a purine salvage pathway, so they are selectively affected. As an add-on to cyclosporine and steroid in kidney transplant it is as good as or better than azathioprine, and should not be combined with it. Adverse effects: vomiting, diarrhoea, leucopenia, CMV infection and GI bleeding. It is contraindicated in pregnancy.

cards.front: Methotrexate in autoimmune disease: what does it do at low dose, and in which conditions is it first-line?
cards.back: It markedly depresses cytokine production and cell-mediated immunity and has anti-inflammatory action. First-line in rapidly progressive rheumatoid arthritis, severe psoriasis, pemphigus, myasthenia gravis, uveitis and chronic active hepatitis. Low-dose maintenance is relatively well tolerated.

cards.front: How do glucocorticoids act as immunosuppressants, and which arm of immunity do they mainly affect?
cards.back: They reduce MHC class II expression, cytokine gene expression (IL-1, IL-2, IL-6) and adhesion molecule production, so helper T-cell activation falls. Their rapid lymphopenia reflects lymphocyte sequestration in tissue. They act mainly on cell-mediated immunity. They are the mainstay for graft-versus-host disease and acute rejection pulses, but long-term toxicity limits use.

cards.front: Etanercept, infliximab and adalimumab: what do they target, and how do they differ?
cards.back: All block TNF. Etanercept is a fusion protein of the TNF receptor and an IgG1 Fc fragment that neutralises TNF. Infliximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody given i.v. every 4 to 8 weeks. Adalimumab is fully human and less antigenic. They are used in rheumatoid arthritis (often with methotrexate), Crohn disease with fistulae, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis and ankylosing spondylitis. Because TNF is needed against granulomatous infection, they raise the risk of tuberculosis and other opportunistic infections; infliximab can induce antinuclear antibodies and rarely a lupus-like syndrome.

cards.front: Complete: anakinra.
cards.text: Anakinra, a recombinant {{IL-1 receptor antagonist}}, is used in refractory rheumatoid arthritis; it is less effective as {{monotherapy}} and is usually given together with {{methotrexate}}.

cards.front: Basiliximab and daclizumab: target, mechanism and use in transplantation.
cards.back: Monoclonal antibodies against CD25, the alpha subunit of the IL-2 receptor on activated T cells; they block IL-2-driven activation and proliferation without lysing the cells. Used for induction in solid-organ transplantation, with steroid, a calcineurin inhibitor and/or azathioprine or mycophenolate. Basiliximab has the higher affinity and a half-life of about 1 week; daclizumab has a longer half-life (about 20 days in GG14, 3 weeks in KDT), but its cost reduced demand and it is now made only for multiple sclerosis. Risks include anaphylaxis, opportunistic infection, oedema and fever.

cards.front: Short note: Muromonab CD3 and antithymocyte globulin

points: Murine antibody to CD3 on T cells; blocks antigen recognition and depletes T cells
Was used for steroid-resistant acute rejection, daily for about 2 weeks with steroid
Repeat courses failed because antibodies formed against the mouse protein
No longer marketed because of its side effects (GG14), though still described in KDT
First dose causes cytokine release syndrome: chills, fever, wheeze, malaise
High-dose steroid pretreatment reduces this
Polyclonal antibody raised in rabbits (or horses) against human thymocytes
Depletes T cells by complement and cell-mediated lysis
Used for induction, for prophylaxis and treatment of acute renal rejection, and for aplastic anaemia
Serum sickness and anaphylaxis

cards.front: Anti-D immunoglobulin: what does it prevent, and when is it given?
cards.back: A human IgG preparation with high titre against the Rh(D) antigen. It is given to Rh(D)-negative women within 72 hours of delivering or aborting an Rh(D)-positive baby, to stop them forming anti-D antibodies that would cause haemolytic disease in later pregnancies. It is also given around the 28th week of pregnancy. Higher doses are needed after accidental transfusion of Rh-positive blood. It is never given to Rh-positive people or to the infant.

cards.front: Essay: Immunosuppression in organ transplantation

points: Antibody induction with an anti-CD25 antibody (basiliximab) or antithymocyte globulin
Triple therapy: calcineurin inhibitor or sirolimus, plus steroid, plus mycophenolate or azathioprine
Calcineurin inhibitors often delayed in kidney transplant to spare the kidney
Three-drug combination of any of: calcineurin inhibitor, sirolimus, steroid, azathioprine or mycophenolate
Drop the component causing toxicity in a given patient
Cyclosporine is often withdrawn after one year, though continuing it reduces acute rejection
Pulse methylprednisolone for acute rejection
If steroid-resistant: antithymocyte globulin (KDT also lists muromonab, now off the market), or rescue with tacrolimus, sirolimus or mycophenolate
Cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil or an anti-CD25 antibody when first-line drugs are not tolerated
Belatacept, a CTLA-4-Ig costimulation blocker, is an i.v. maintenance option in kidney transplant with better renal function than cyclosporine
Bacterial, fungal and viral (especially CMV) and opportunistic infection
Lymphoma and other malignancy after a long latency, from weakened immune surveillance

cards.front: What are the two general adverse effects of immunosuppressive therapy?
cards.back: Increased risk of bacterial, fungal and viral (especially cytomegalovirus) and other opportunistic infections; and development of lymphoma and other malignancies after a long latency, because immune surveillance is weakened.

cards.front: Short note: Tretinoin and arsenic trioxide in acute promyelocytic leukaemia

points: Most APL carries the t(15;17) translocation fusing PML with the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene; the fusion protein blocks myeloid differentiation
At pharmacological concentrations it switches on the differentiation programme and promotes degradation of PML-RARA
Alone it reverses the bleeding tendency and gives temporary remission; with an anthracycline, long relapse-free survival in most patients
Cleared by CYP3A4: inducers cause resistance; azole inhibitors can cause hypercalcaemia and renal failure
Raises reactive oxygen species and triggers apoptosis; also degrades PML-RARA
Highly effective in relapsed APL; now combined with tretinoin first-line, with an anthracycline added in high-risk cases (KDT: WBC above 10,000/microlitre)
Differentiation syndrome: fever, dyspnoea, weight gain, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural or pericardial effusion; corticosteroids prevent or treat it
Tretinoin: dry skin, cheilitis, raised lipids and liver enzymes, pseudotumor cerebri
Arsenic: QT prolongation (check and replete potassium), hyperglycaemia

cards.front: Complete: protective (rescue) agents paired with the drug whose toxicity they prevent.
cards.text: Mesna protects the bladder from {{ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide}}; leucovorin rescues normal cells after high-dose {{methotrexate}}; dexrazoxane reduces cardiotoxicity of {{doxorubicin}}; amifostine protects against renal and neural toxicity of {{cisplatin}}; rasburicase treats acute hyperuricaemia from {{rapid tumour lysis}}; uridine triacetate rescues {{fluorouracil}} toxicity in DPD deficiency.

cards.front: Which anticancer drugs have cumulative-dose limits, and what toxicity does each limit prevent?
cards.back: Doxorubicin: cardiomyopathy, usual total limit about 550 mg/m2 (about 300 mg/m2 in children); epirubicin above 900 mg/m2. Bleomycin: pulmonary fibrosis; KDT keeps the total under 250 mg, and GG14 advises caution beyond that. Cisplatin: nephrotoxicity that depends on the total dose. Etoposide: weekly or twice-weekly dosing above a cumulative 2000 mg/m2 raises the risk of secondary leukaemia. Busulfan: pulmonary fibrosis with long-term use.

cards.front: Short note: Hormones and related agents in cancer therapy

points: Hormonal agents are not cytotoxic; they slow hormone-dependent tumours
Effects are palliative; they block hormone signalling or lower hormone levels
Tamoxifen (SERM): adjuvant for 5 years, then an aromatase inhibitor
Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole): first-line in advanced hormone-receptor-positive disease
Fulvestrant (SERD): used with CDK4/6 inhibitors in advanced disease
GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin) or antagonists (degarelix, relugolix) suppress testosterone
Antiandrogens (flutamide, bicalutamide) given with a GnRH analogue or orchiectomy
Estrogens superseded; abiraterone blocks steroid synthesis and is given with prednisone
High-dose progestins give temporary remission in endometrial cancer
Glucocorticoids (prednisolone, dexamethasone) in acute childhood leukaemia, lymphomas and Hodgkin palliation

cards.front: Essay: Antimetabolites in cancer chemotherapy

points: Structural analogues of folate, purines or pyrimidines
They compete with normal substrates or get incorporated into DNA or RNA, forming dysfunctional molecules
Mostly S-phase specific
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthase
Folinic acid rescue reverses toxicity; folic acid does not
Pemetrexed mainly inhibits thymidylate synthase; hand-foot rash is common
Mercaptopurine and thioguanine block purine interconversion and enter nucleic acids; used in childhood acute leukaemia
Allopurinol raises toxicity of mercaptopurine and azathioprine; TPMT deficiency increases toxicity
Fludarabine is used in CLL and lymphoma that has relapsed
Fluorouracil irreversibly inhibits thymidylate synthase and enters RNA; DPD deficiency causes severe toxicity
Cytarabine inhibits DNA polymerase and acts in S phase
Bone marrow depression, mucositis and diarrhoea are common
Low-dose methotrexate causes megaloblastic anaemia; high dose causes pancytopenia
Hyperuricaemia occurs with antipurines

cards.front: Short note: Immunostimulants

points: Anthelmintic (ascariasis, second line) that also restores depressed T-cell function
Earlier used in rheumatoid arthritis and as an adjunct in malignancy; no longer used because repeated doses produce severe reactions
Topical TLR-7 agonist that induces interferon-alpha
Used topically for superficial basal cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis and genital warts
BCG, an attenuated live vaccine, given intravesically for superficial bladder cancer
Intravenous immunoglobulin is a pooled preparation of antibodies from plasma donors

refs: Bennett & Brown Clin Pharmacol PDF p276

cards.front: Short note: Calcineurin inhibitors (immunosuppressants)

points: Cyclosporine: cyclic polypeptide of 11 amino acids obtained from a fungus
Calcineurin inhibitors are one of the immunosuppressant groups described in KDT8 (ch65)

cards.front: Short note: Immunomodulators

points: Drugs that alter the immune response: some suppress it (immunosuppressants), others restore depressed function (immunostimulants)
Levamisole restores depressed T-cell function
Leflunomide: inhibits proliferation of stimulated lymphocytes in active RA
Sulfasalazine: anti-inflammatory; a sulfapyridine plus 5-aminosalicylic acid compound
Anthelmintic that was used in RA and as an adjunct in malignancy
Repeated doses produce severe reactions, so it is no longer used for these
JAK inhibitors (JAKinibs) act as immunomodulators
Used in ulcerative colitis, psoriasis, myelofibrosis and polycythaemia vera

cards.front: Short note: Cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide: bladder toxicity and mesna

points: Cyclophosphamide: oral 2 to 3 mg/kg/day; i.v. 10 to 15 mg/kg every 7 to 10 days
Ifosfamide: longer, dose-dependent half-life
Caused by acrolein-type metabolites in urine
Mesna (sulfhydryl) given with ifosfamide; bladder irrigation with acetylcysteine

cards.front: Short note: Methotrexate: high dose and rescue

points: S-phase specific; 50% plasma protein bound
Largely excreted unchanged in urine
Folinic acid rescue allows much higher doses
Folic acid cannot reverse toxicity (not converted to active coenzyme)
15 to 30 mg/day orally for 5 days, or 20 to 40 mg/m2 twice weekly; apparently curative

cards.front: What is the dose-limiting toxicity of oxaliplatin, and how does it differ from cisplatin?
cards.back: Peripheral neuropathy (sensory paraesthesia of arms, legs, mouth and throat); cisplatin's main problem is renal impairment, and oxaliplatin is active where cisplatin resistance has developed.

cards.front: Why is cisplatin given with routine antiemetics?
cards.back: It is highly emetic, so antiemetics are given before each infusion; its most important dose-limiting toxicity is renal impairment.

cards.front: Which alkylating agent spares myeloid tissue, and what is its dose?
cards.back: Chlorambucil, which is slow acting and mainly affects lymphoid tissue; 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg daily for 3 to 6 weeks, then 2 mg daily maintenance.

cards.front: Why do taxanes need premedication?
cards.back: Paclitaxel uses a polyoxyethylated castor oil vehicle that causes anaphylactoid reactions, so dexamethasone and H1/H2 blockers are given beforehand.
